core_principles: Incorporate anterolateral 45-degree resistance during partial lunges to selectively increase the vastus medialis oblique (VMO) to vastus lateralis (VL) activation ratio.
Balancing VMO and VL muscle activity is critical for proper patellar tracking and preventing or managing patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS).
Avoid pure lateral (90-degree) resistance if the goal is to maximize the VMO/VL activation ratio, as it is less effective than anterolateral 45-degree resistance.
common_mistakes: Allowing an imbalance between the VMO and VL muscles, which causes lateral patellar displacement and increased joint pressure.
specific_findings: The study evaluated 22 healthy participants with no knee pain, limitation of motion, or history of lower extremity surgery.
The VMO/VL EMG activity ratio during lunge with anterolateral 45° resistance was significantly higher than with no resistance and lateral 90° resistance (p < 0.05).
There was no significant difference in VMO, VL, and VMO/VL muscle activity between male and female subjects (p > 0.05).

core_principles: Perform a partial lunge by lowering the body to approximately 50 degrees of knee flexion, which is highly suitable for early-stage rehabilitation.
Keep the upper body upright during the lunge.
Set the front ankle at approximately 60 degrees of abduction to increase Vastus Medialis Oblique (VMO) muscle activation.
Apply resistance from an anterolateral 45-degree angle to selectively increase the VMO to Vastus Lateralis (VL) activation ratio.
Use visual feedback (e.g., a mirror) or light external support to prevent the center of gravity from shifting sideways when resistance is applied.
common_mistakes: Shifting the center of gravity excessively toward the direction of lateral resistance during the lunge.
specific_findings: Study analyzed 21 healthy young adults (mean age 20.75 ± 2.28 years).
Ankle abduction angle of 60 degrees increases VMO activation during lunges.
Partial lunge was performed to 50 degrees of knee flexion.

Anterolateral 45-degree resistance resulted in a significantly higher VMO/VL EMG activity ratio (125.31 ± 20.74% MVIC) compared to no resistance (111.71 ± 21.59% MVIC) and lateral 90-degree resistance (113.16 ± 24.75% MVIC) (p < 0.05).
VMO muscle activation was 58.02 ± 19.71% MVIC with 45-degree resistance, compared to 47.75 ± 18.12% MVIC with no resistance and 46.45 ± 16.83% MVIC with 90-degree resistance.
